title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate P of finite simple undirected graphs on \([n]\), decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing P has worst-case round complexity \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\)? Only node 1 is required to output the decision bit, and the input, bandwidth and limiting convention are fixed below.
why: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
status_note: The checked primary literature leaves explicit superconstant unicast bounds as a central challenge. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution of this polynomial-time, one-bit target. The latest checked revision of the one-round MST result is January 2024; it is not presented as a new 2026 status theorem.
review_note: Preserved the proposal’s centralized polynomial-time restriction and strict \(\omega (1)\) notation. Specified labeled graph inputs, uniform deterministic algorithms, logarithmic per-link messages, unrestricted local computation and designated-node output. Source review distinguishes stronger or weaker models and does not independently audit the cited proofs.

progress.text: Circuit simulations explain barriers to explicit lower bounds and separate unicast from broadcast communication.
A uniform congested-clique time hierarchy is proved through hard-function selection, without the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time guarantee.
The MST lower bound excludes one round with logarithmic link bandwidth; it does not establish a diverging lower bound for a one-bit graph predicate.

references.locator: PODC 2023; revision 4, 31 January 2024 abstract. One-round MST algorithms require Ω(log³ n) link bandwidth, hence at least two rounds with O(log n) messages; a constant lower bound and a multi-edge output task.

importance.reason: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.

category_assignment.reason: Category from the approved fundamental-problem proposal

sentences: Can a graph predicate that is easy to compute centrally require a number of congested-clique rounds tending to infinity?
Each processor initially knows its incident graph edges and can send a different logarithmic-size message to every other processor in each round.
Only one decision bit is required, and local computation is unrestricted.
Known hard-function counting and hierarchy arguments do not provide the required centrally polynomial-time predicate.
Broadcast bounds and the known two-round MST limitation do not resolve this unicast one-bit target.

upgraded_from.title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique

definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(\mathrm{P}(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: The network and the input graph differ
context_blocks.text: Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

context_blocks.title: One bit can be much easier than collecting the input
context_blocks.text: For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

context_blocks.title: Why unicast is essential
context_blocks.text: In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

context_blocks.title: The explicitness requirement
context_blocks.text: Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

context_blocks.title: Connections and known limitations
context_blocks.text: The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker \(\omega (1)\) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.
